prompt.context: Your client is the New York City Transit system, also known as the MTA. Specifically, you are working for the subway division. This division is part of a government authority that operates all the subways in New York City. Recently, the division approached you because they have been operating at a net loss. How can you help this client?
prompt.question: How can you help the MTA understand its current ridership and profitability drivers?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current ticket price?
clarifying_info.a: The price for a single ride ticket is $2.75. Ticket options include single rides, weekly pass, monthly pass, and reduced (for students and elderly).

clarifying_info.q: How many train lines does the MTA have?
clarifying_info.a: There are 22 train lines on the MTA (e.g., 1-7, A-G, J, L, M, N, Q, R, W, Z).

clarifying_info.q: Does the MTA receive government funding?
clarifying_info.a: The MTA gets current funding from ticket sales as well as some government funding. Government funding can be ignored for this case.

clarifying_info.q: Should we focus on revenues, costs, or both?
clarifying_info.a: Because expenses are largely fixed by contract (e.g., unions), the case will be focused on revenues.

framework: Estimate market size (ridership) — either capacity-based (number of lines, cars, volume per car) or demand-based (NYC population, % who take subways)

Identify profitability drivers — Revenue: ticket price (single ride, weekly/monthly passes) and volume; Cost: variable (electricity, new construction) and fixed (labor/unions, infrastructure/depreciation)

questions.prompt: How would you estimate the total number of subway rides taken on an average weekday in New York City?
questions.guidance: Candidate should choose either a capacity-based or demand-based approach and state their assumption. The model solution uses a capacity-based build-up from lines to cars to capacity to train frequency.

math.setup: Build up from: 22 lines × 10 cars/train × 100 people/car = 1,000 people per train. Rush hour: trains every 5 min → 12 trains/hour. Non-rush: trains every 10 min → 6 trains/hour. But the casebook uses 20 trains/hour for rush and 10 trains/hour for non-rush (likely counting both directions or both termini); use casebook figures.
steps: Rush hour: 20 trains/hour × 6 hours × 1,000 people/train × 22 lines = 2,640,000
math.answer: ~6,600,000 rides per weekday (consistent with ~6 million officially reported by the MTA)

questions.prompt: Because of the nature of their expenses (pensions, union contracts, required maintenance), the MTA has asked you to help them turn around their profitability by focusing on opportunities to grow revenues. What are some ways for the MTA to grow their revenues?
questions.guidance: Strong answers separate short-term levers (pricing) from long-term levers (capacity expansion, policy) and give specific, actionable ideas within each bucket.

questions.prompt: Given that the MTA is a public agency with a public mission, what are some concerns if the MTA adopts a distance-based pricing scheme?
questions.guidance: Candidate should consider two dimensions: impact to riders (equity/income distribution) and impact to the city (real estate, congestion, ridership mix). Strong answers quantify or at least directionally reason through each effect.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways for the MTA to grow their revenues?

categories.name: Short-term — Ticket pricing
ideas: Create distance-based pricing (charge more for longer rides)
Create demand-based pricing (e.g., higher fares during rush hour)
Reduce or restrict unlimited pass options

categories.name: Short-term — Ticket volume
ideas: Conduct advertising campaign to attract new riders
Promotions or partnerships to drive ridership

categories.name: Long-term — Expand coverage and services
ideas: Add more service to high-demand lines
Build new lines into up-and-coming neighborhoods

categories.name: Long-term — Policy and funding
ideas: Lobby for greater taxes on alternative transportation (driving, taxis)
Advocate for additional government funding for subways

recommendation: Introduce new pricing schemes, including distance-based or demand-based pricing, to grow MTA revenues
Differentiated pricing would better match demand (by distance or time) to available supply (train capacity)
risks: A demand-based pricing scheme could deviate from the MTA's public mission by disproportionately impacting lower-income riders who commute farther
Implementation of price differentiation requires significant infrastructure upgrades (e.g., to track system entry and exit)
next_steps: Conduct analysis to understand the impact of any pricing change on different areas and populations of the city
Determine appropriate pricing levels for the new scheme
Work with local officials and community representatives to solicit input and feedback
